html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Describe security through the lifecycle phases, and the older 4 Cs
  • Trace an API request through authentication, authorization and admission
  • Grant access with RBAC and ServiceAccounts, using least privilege
  • Apply Pod Security Standards, securityContext and supply chain controls

2The CNCF lifecycle phases and the 4 Cs of older material

Running case

Harbor Books Locks the Doors

  • Developers may look at Pods in the shop namespace, but only the delivery pipeline may change them
  • The orders Pods must run with as few privileges as possible
  • Only trusted, checked images may run, and the payment key must stay secret
  • In this module you decide who may do what, and what a Pod may do

Security Through the Lifecycle

  • The current docs follow the CNCF's lifecycle phases: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime
  • Develop: a threat model, code review, and zero trust: never trust, always verify
  • Distribute: secure the supply chain: scan images, use certificates or signatures, keep a private registry
  • Deploy: control what is deployed, who deploys it and where
  • Runtime: protect access, compute and storage

Exam tip: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime: security follows the software through its life.

The 4 Cs of Cloud Native Security Old wording

  • Older Kubernetes docs and study material describe the 4 Cs: Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code
  • Security is layered: each layer builds on the layer outside it
  • Strong outer layers help the inner ones; weak outer layers cannot be repaired in code
  • The current docs use the lifecycle phases, so know both vocabularies

Exam tip: 4 Cs: Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code, from the outside in.

3The API request path, authentication, authorization, admission

The API Request Path

  • A request meets TLS, then three checks in order: authentication, authorization, admission
  • Authentication: who are you? Client certificates, tokens, bootstrap tokens and JWTs for service accounts; failure gives 401
  • Authorization: what may you do? RBAC is the usual mode; denial gives 403
  • Admission: may modify or reject objects being created, changed or deleted; it never acts on reads
  • Kubernetes has no User object: users come from outside

Exam tip: Who are you, what may you do, is the object acceptable.

4RBAC, roles and bindings, least privilege

RBAC: Roles and Bindings

  • Role: permissions in one namespace; ClusterRole: not namespaced, for cluster-wide or cluster-scoped resources
  • RoleBinding: gives a role to subjects (users, groups, ServiceAccounts) in a namespace; ClusterRoleBinding: cluster-wide
  • A RoleBinding can point at a ClusterRole to reuse it inside one namespace
  • Permissions are additive: there are no deny rules
  • Least privilege: avoid wildcards, and keep cluster-admin for when it is truly needed

Exam tip: A role says what, a binding says to whom, and nothing denies.

An RBAC Role

  • A rule names apiGroups, resources and verbs; the empty string is the core group
  • Common verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, delete
  • resourceNames narrows a rule to named objects
  • A RoleBinding then gives this Role to a user, group or ServiceAccount

Read-only access to Pods and their logs in the shop namespace

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: shop
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

Exam tip: A Role lists what is allowed; the binding says to whom.

5ServiceAccounts

ServiceAccounts

ServiceAccount User
For Pods and automation people
Lives as an API object in a namespace outside Kubernetes; there is no User object
Credential a short-lived, rotating token through the TokenRequest API certificates, tokens and other methods
  • Every namespace gets a default ServiceAccount when it is created
  • A Pod runs as a ServiceAccount, and you give that account permissions with RBAC
  • automountServiceAccountToken: false stops a Pod from mounting a token, for Pods that never call the API

Exam tip: ServiceAccounts are for Pods; users are for people.

6Admission webhooks, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, policy engines

Admission Control and Policy Engines Beyond the curriculum

  • Admission controllers run after authentication and authorization, and before the object is stored
  • They may mutate (set defaults) or validate (accept or reject); only mutating ones change the object
  • Webhooks: mutating first, then validating
  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is a built-in, declarative option for validation, with rules in the Common Expression Language (CEL)
  • Policy engines such as Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper and Kyverno enforce rules through admission

Exam tip: Admission sees changes to objects, never reads.

7Pod Security Standards, Pod Security Admission, securityContext

Pod Security Standards and Admission

Level What it allows
Privileged unrestricted; allows known privilege escalations
Baseline minimally restrictive; prevents known privilege escalations
Restricted heavily restricted, following current hardening best practices
  • Pod Security admission is the built-in controller that applies a level to a namespace, with labels such as pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
  • The mode decides the effect: enforce rejects the Pod, audit adds an audit annotation, warn shows a warning
  • PodSecurityPolicy is gone; Pod Security admission replaces it

Exam tip: The level says how strict; the mode says what happens.

securityContext

  • A securityContext sets privilege and access settings for a Pod, or for one container
  • A container's settings override the Pod's where they overlap
  • Common settings: run as non-root, no privilege escalation, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, a seccomp profile
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation is true when you leave it unset

A locked-down orders container

securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
containers:
- name: orders
  image: orders:stable
  securityContext:
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}

Exam tip: Drop everything the container does not need.

8Secrets and network controls, image supply chain, runtime security and auditing, what the exam asks

Protecting Secrets and Traffic

Control What it does
Secrets enable encryption at rest, limit access with least-privilege RBAC, and consider an external secret store; base64 is not encryption
TLS protects traffic to the Kubernetes API
NetworkPolicy limits which Pods may talk to which (Module 6); needs a plugin that enforces it
Service mesh can encrypt and authenticate traffic between services with mutual TLS (Module 6)
  • Granting list on Secrets lets the holder read their contents

Exam tip: Defense in depth: no single control is enough.

Image Supply Chain Security Beyond the curriculum

  • Scan images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs); a scanner such as Trivy also lists the packages inside, an SBOM
  • Sign images and verify the signature before use: Cosign, from Sigstore, signs container images
  • Keep images in a private registry that lets only authorized clients pull
  • At deploy time an admission policy, for example in Kyverno, can verify signatures

Exam tip: Scan, sign, store privately, verify at admission.

Runtime Security and Auditing Beyond the curriculum

Tool What it does
seccomp filters the system calls a process may make
AppArmor restricts programs with profiles
Falco a CNCF graduated tool that watches kernel events such as system calls against rules, and alerts on abnormal behavior
Audit log a chronological record of API actions, with levels None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse

Exam tip: Restrict with seccomp and AppArmor, detect with Falco, record with the audit log.

What the Exam Asks: Security

  • Authentication, authorization or admission: who you are, what you may do, whether the object is acceptable
  • Role or ClusterRole: one namespace, or cluster-wide; a RoleBinding can reuse a ClusterRole in one namespace
  • RBAC rules: additive, with no deny
  • ServiceAccount or user: Pods and a namespaced object, or people and external
  • Pod Security level or mode: Privileged, Baseline, Restricted; enforce, audit, warn
  • Lifecycle phases or 4 Cs: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime now; Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code in older material

Exam tip: For a security question, find the layer first: identity, permission, admission, Pod or supply chain.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Which four lifecycle phases of cloud native security do the current Kubernetes docs use?

  • ACloud, Clusters, Containers and Code, each one built on the layer outside it
  • BPlan, Build, Test and Release, each one run by the delivery pipeline of the team
  • CIdentify, Protect, Detect and Respond, each one owned by a separate security team
  • DDevelop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime, which follow the software through its life
Show the answer

Answer: D. The current docs follow the CNCF lifecycle phases: Develop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime. Cloud, Clusters, Containers and Code are the 4 Cs of older material.

S2In which order does the API server check an incoming request?

  • AAdmission, then authorization, then authentication of the user who sent the request
  • BAuthentication, then authorization, then admission, before the object is stored
  • CAuthorization, then authentication, then admission, because roles come first
  • DAuthentication, then admission, then authorization, so that policies see the user
Show the answer

Answer: B. The request is authenticated first, so the cluster knows who is asking, then authorized, so it knows what that user may do, and finally passed through admission control, which can modify or reject the object.

S3Harbor Books wants developers to read Pods only in the shop namespace. Which objects achieve this?

  • AA Role that allows get, list and watch on Pods in shop, and a RoleBinding to the developers
  • BA ClusterRole that allows every verb on every resource, and a ClusterRoleBinding to the developers
  • CA ServiceAccount for each developer, with the default token mounted into the Pods of the namespace
  • DA NetworkPolicy that selects the Pods of shop and allows traffic from the developers' laptops
Show the answer

Answer: A. A Role limits permissions to one namespace, and a RoleBinding gives it to the developers. A cluster-wide role breaks least privilege, ServiceAccounts are for workloads, and a NetworkPolicy does not control API permissions.

S4Which statement about RBAC permissions is correct?

  • AA deny rule in a ClusterRole overrides every allow rule that applies to the same user
  • BA RoleBinding can never refer to a ClusterRole, because a binding is tied to Roles
  • CPermissions are purely additive, and RBAC has no deny rules
  • DA Role is a cluster-scoped object that can be bound only through a ClusterRoleBinding
Show the answer

Answer: C. RBAC permissions only add up: the rules of all applicable roles are combined and there are no deny rules. A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole to reuse it in one namespace, and a Role is namespaced.

S5A Harbor Books Pod never calls the Kubernetes API. How can the team reduce the risk from its API credential?

  • ASet automountServiceAccountToken to false in the Pod spec, so that no token is mounted
  • BBind the Pod's ServiceAccount to cluster-admin, so that the API can never deny it anything
  • CCreate a User object for the Pod in the API, and let the Pod log in with a password
  • DDelete the namespace and create it again, so that a new default token is created
Show the answer

Answer: A. Turning off the automatic mount means the Pod holds no API token that an attacker could steal. Granting cluster-admin does the opposite, Kubernetes has no User object, and recreating the namespace does not change how tokens are mounted.

S6What can a mutating admission webhook do that a validating admission webhook cannot?

  • ACheck who sent the request before any other part of the API server does
  • BBlock get and list requests, because reads pass through admission control too
  • CReplace the RBAC rules of the cluster while the request is being processed
  • DModify the object in the request, for example by setting defaults
Show the answer

Answer: D. Mutating admission may change the object, and validating admission may only accept or reject it. Authentication comes earlier, and admission does not act on reads.

S7Which Pod Security admission mode rejects a Pod that violates the chosen level?

  • Aaudit, which adds an annotation to the audit log and still allows the Pod
  • Benforce, which rejects the Pod
  • Cwarn, which shows a warning to the user and still allows the Pod
  • Dbaseline, which blocks every Pod that asks for more than the default settings
Show the answer

Answer: B. The enforce mode rejects violating Pods. Audit and warn allow them, and baseline is a level, not a mode.

S8The Harbor Books orders Pods must not gain extra privileges, and must not write to their root filesystem. Which securityContext settings do this?

  • Aprivileged set to true, and runAsUser set to zero, so the container owns its files
  • BhostNetwork set to true, and hostPID set to true, so the container can see the node
  • CallowPrivilegeEscalation set to false, and readOnlyRootFilesystem set to true
  • DpriorityClassName set to a high value, and a memory limit set on every container
Show the answer

Answer: C. Setting allowPrivilegeEscalation to false stops a process from gaining more privileges, and setting readOnlyRootFilesystem to true makes the root filesystem read-only. The other options widen access or have nothing to do with a container's privileges.

S9Which tool watches kernel events such as system calls and alerts on abnormal behavior at runtime?

  • ACosign, which signs container images and checks the signatures later
  • BFalco, a runtime security tool that applies rules to kernel events
  • CTrivy, which scans images for known vulnerabilities and lists their packages
  • DKyverno, a policy engine that validates and mutates objects at admission
Show the answer

Answer: B. Falco watches kernel events against rules and raises alerts at runtime. Cosign signs images, Trivy scans them, and Kyverno enforces policies at admission.
